events.c: The captain and first officer received a briefing using an earlier flight plan. The exact time is unknown.
The destination route point moved east before departure. The crew were not told.
The aircraft left Auckland for Antarctic sightseeing, with its first return landing planned at Christchurch.
The crew received a forecast of cloud and occasional light snow that could reduce visibility near McMurdo.
The captain proposed an early descent while about 144 miles north of McMurdo.
A forecaster reported low cloud around 2,000 feet near McMurdo. Clearer areas were far to the northwest.
The first officer requested a lower altitude. Air traffic control cleared descent to a higher level than requested.
The aircraft began descending. Its altitude and speed guidance worked normally.
Air traffic control offered radar guidance down to 1,500 feet, but radar never identified the aircraft.
The crew accepted radar guidance for descent. Radio contact and navigation distance readings later remained unreliable.
The aircraft automatically leveled off at its selected pressure altitude. This did not measure height above terrain.
The captain spotted a break in the cloud and proposed circling to descend.
The crew switched from following the programmed route to selecting headings. The autopilot began a descending right turn.
Air traffic control approved descent by sight and required altitude reports. Radar provided no terrain clearance.
A ground controller requested restarting the aircraft's radar identification transmitter and setting its identification code.
The first officer reported continued descent and confirmed the request for radar guidance. Radar never located the aircraft.
The first officer reported 10,000 feet, but the aircraft was about 9,400 feet high because of incorrect settings.
The captain proposed another circle to keep flying by sight. The aircraft turned left.
The first officer requested descent away from Ross Island, then an approach by sight. It later turned back.
Air traffic control required sufficient visibility to fly by sight and continued altitude reports.
The crew selected automatic airspeed control while descending through the second left turn.
The captain prepared the navigation guidance to resume following the programmed route.
The autopilot resumed following the programmed route, which now led toward Mount Erebus's northern slopes.
The first officer reported descending from 6,000 toward 2,000 feet. The aircraft was actually at 5,400 feet.
Air traffic control acknowledged the altitude report. Later radio calls received no successful reply.
The captain read the local pressure setting. The altitude instruments were corrected before the final low approach.
The captain selected 260 knots. Engine power stayed low until the aircraft slowed to that speed.
After briefly leveling near 2,000 feet, the captain requested descent to 1,500 feet without informing air traffic control.
The aircraft began holding altitude at 1,515 feet, with small changes in height afterward.
The captain announced plans to climb away while the crew discussed turn direction. A climb remained unconfirmed.
About 11 seconds before impact, the aircraft crossed a coastal ice cliff. Rising terrain sharply reduced ground clearance.
About eight seconds before impact, selected heading guidance replaced route following. The aircraft began banking right.
The terrain warning sounded about six and a half seconds before impact. The system worked as designed.
About four seconds before impact, a sharp nose-up control movement apparently disconnected the autopilot.
About three and a half seconds before impact, the right bank peaked, then reversed. Left rudder was applied.
The flight engineer called decreasing height above terrain. The captain requested engine power to escape.
The aircraft struck the ice slope before achieving a significant climb. All 257 aboard died.
Search aircraft found the wreckage about 11 hours after impact.
The first investigation attributed the crash to continuing at low altitude and failing to detect rising terrain.
The Royal Commission blamed the unannounced route change and defective airline procedures, clearing the crew of contributing error.
The appeal failed. Findings about the crash went unchallenged, while the legal costs order remained overturned for unfairness.
The government accepted the Royal Commission's findings. Government and airline apologies addressed their failures and treatment of families.
Services in Christchurch, Auckland and at Scott Base marked the crash's 45th anniversary.
Cracroft Reserve in Christchurch was chosen for the memorial after a search for an Auckland site.
A memorial concept design adapted for Cracroft Reserve was released.
Construction followed a site blessing and groundbreaking in June 2026. The memorial's unveiling was still pending.

one_line: A sightseeing aircraft struck Mount Erebus after an unannounced route change and loss of terrain contrast.
status_why: The collision sequence is established, but two official inquiries differed over the roles of crew decisions and airline failures.
